I was executing well — member experience, managing the front office rhythm, using Salesforce daily — but I had genuinely mastered what the role had to offer. Working in hotel operations for several years, I had seen first-hand how a badly handled PMS migration can destabilise a whole property. Soho House was a great environment, but it wasn't going to get me there. So I moved deliberately.

rows.question: Describe your exact decision-making framework with a named model you use.
rows.answer:
That's not really how I work, and I'd rather give you an honest picture than dress it up as a framework.

I don't use a named model — no "MECE", no "First Principles", no acronym I reach for. What I actually do is closer to: slow down before touching anything, separate what someone believes is happening from what the data shows, find the constraint that actually matters, and then work from there.

The clearest example I can give is the consulting engagement I'm on now. The owner had a working theory about where revenue was leaking. My first move was deliberately not to act on it — I ran a structured discovery process first, with interview scripts and templates, specifically to test whether the beliefs matched reality. Some did. Several didn't. The stacked discounts on Booking.com — Genius levels compounding on top of a mobile rate — were invisible to the owner because nobody had ever looked at it that way. That surfaced from the data, not from the intuition.

So if there's a thread through how I make decisions, it's probably: diagnose before prescribing, and treat the obvious solution as a hypothesis, not an answer. Ripping out a legacy PMS, for instance, was the obvious move on that engagement. The interesting question was what we could get out of the existing system first — and it turned out the channel manager they were already paying for had never been switched on.

That's the honest version. No framework name attached to it.
rows.reason: The candidate explicitly declined to name a framework and instead described their actual approach in general terms, which aligns with the pass criterion that no named framework exists in their verified data.
